tool_calls.result: 83.491 Fee in lieu of security deposit. — (1)(a) If a rental agreement requires a security deposit, a landlord may offer a tenant the option to pay a fee in lieu of a security deposit. (b) A landlord may provide a tenant the option of paying a security deposit in monthly installments in an amount that is agreed upon between the tenant and the landlord while participating in the fee program. (2)(a) If a tenant agrees to pay a fee in lieu of a security deposit, the landlord must notify the tenant within 30 days after the conclusion of the tenancy if there are any costs or fees due resulting from unpaid rent, fees, or other obligations under the rental agreement, including, but not limited to, costs required for repairing damage to the premises beyond normal wear and tear. (b) A landlord may not submit a claim to an insurer to recover the landlord’s losses associated with unpaid rent, fees, or other obligations under the rental agreement, including, but not limited to, costs required for repairing damage to the premises beyond normal wear and tear, until at least 15 days after providing the tenant with the required notice under paragraph (a). 1. The landlord must include an itemized list of any unpaid amounts and the dates such amounts were due, documentation supporting any itemized damages and costs of repairs, and a copy of any written objection or report of any communication of objection by the tenant when the landlord submits a claim to an insurer. 2. If an insurer pays a claim that was submitted under this subsection to a landlord and the insurer has subrogation rights, the insurer may, within 1 year after the tenancy that was the subject of the claim ends, seek reimbursement from the tenant for the amounts paid to the landlord. If the insurer seeks reimbursement from the tenant, the following apply: a. The insurer must provide the tenant with all documentation for losses which the landlord provided to the insurer in support of the landlord’s claim and a copy of the settlement statement documenting the insurer’s payment of the landlord’s claim. b. The tenant retains any defenses against the insurer which the tenant would otherwise have against the landlord. 3. A landlord may not accept payment from both a tenant and an insurer for amounts associated with the same rent, fees, or damages. (3) If a landlord offers a tenant the option to pay a fee in lieu of a security deposit, the landlord must notify the tenant in writing of all of the following: (a) That the tenant has the option to pay a security deposit instead of the fee at any time. (b) That the tenant may, at any time, terminate the agreement to pay the fee in lieu of the security deposit and instead pay a security deposit as listed in a rental agreement between the landlord and tenant or, if a security deposit was not agreed upon in a rental agreement between the landlord and tenant, in the amount that is otherwise offered to new tenants for a substantially similar dwelling unit on the date that the tenant terminates the agreement. (c) That the tenant may choose to pay the security deposit in monthly installments in an amount that is agreed upon between the landlord and tenant while participating in the fee program. (d) Whether any additional charges apply for the options provided in paragraphs (a) and (b). (e) The amount of the payments required for each option the landlord offers. (f) That the fee is nonrefundable, if applicable. (g) That the fee is only for securing occupancy without paying a required security deposit. (h) That the fee payment does not limit or change the tenant’s obligation to pay rent and fees, if any, under the rental agreement or limit or change the tenant’s obligation to pay the costs of repairing damage to the premises beyond normal wear and tear. (i) That if the landlord uses any portion of the fee to purchase insurance, the tenant is not insured and is not a beneficiary of the landlord’s insurance coverage, and that the insurance does not limit or change the tenant’s obligations to pay rent and fees under the rental agreement or change the tenant’s obligation to pay the costs of repairing damage to the premises beyond normal wear and tear. (4)(a) If a tenant decides to pay a fee in lieu of a security deposit, a written agreement to collect the fee must be signed by the landlord, or the landlord’s agent, and the tenant. The written agreement may not contain any clause that contradicts s. 83.45 or s. 83.47 . The written agreement must, at a minimum, specify all of the following: 1. The amount of the fee, which may not be increased during the term of the rental agreement. 2. How and when the fee is to be collected. 3. The process and timeframe during which a tenant must pay the security deposit specified in the rental agreement if the tenant defaults on paying the fee, and that such default will not adversely affect the tenant’s credit rating if the security deposit is timely paid. 4. That the written agreement may be terminated at any time as long as the tenant pays the amount of the security deposit specified in the rental agreement. 5. If the tenant pays the amount of the security deposit specified in the rental agreement, then the tenant’s default on paying the fee or termination of the written agreement may not adversely impact the tenant’s credit report. (b) The written agreement specified under paragraph (a) must also include a disclosure in substantially the following form: FEE IN LIEU OF SECURITY DEPOSIT THIS FEE IS NOT A SECURITY DEPOSIT AND PAYMENT OF THE FEE DOES NOT ABSOLVE THE TENANT OF ANY OBLIGATIONS UNDER THE RENTAL AGREEMENT, INCLUDING THE OBLIGATION TO PAY RENT AS IT BECOMES DUE AND ANY COSTS AND DAMAGES BEYOND NORMAL WEAR AND TEAR WHICH THE TENANT OR HIS OR HER GUESTS MAY CAUSE. THE TENANT MAY TERMINATE THIS AGREEMENT AT ANY TIME AND STOP PAYING THE FEE AND INSTEAD PAY THE SECURITY DEPOSIT AS PROVIDED IN SECTION 83.491 , FLORIDA STATUTES. THIS AGREEMENT HAS BEEN ENTERED INTO VOLUNTARILY BY BOTH PARTIES AND THE TENANT AGREES TO PAY THE LANDLORD A FEE IN LIEU OF A SECURITY DEPOSIT AS AUTHORIZED UNDER SECTION 83.491 , FLORIDA STATUTES. IF THE LANDLORD USES ANY PORTION OF THE TENANT’S FEE TO PURCHASE INSURANCE, THE TENANT IS NOT INSURED AND IS NOT A BENEFICIARY OF SUCH COVERAGE, AND THE INSURANCE DOES NOT CHANGE THE TENANT’S FINANCIAL OBLIGATIONS UNDER THE RENTAL AGREEMENT. THIS DISCLOSURE IS BASIC. PLEASE REFER TO PART II OF CHAPTER 83, FLORIDA STATUTES, TO DETERMINE YOUR LEGAL RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS. (5) A fee in lieu of a security deposit may be: (a) A recurring monthly fee, payable on the same date that the rent payment is due under the rental agreement; or (b) Payable upon a schedule that the landlord and tenant choose and as specified in the written agreement. (6) A fee collected under this section, or an insurance product or a surety bond accepted, by a landlord in lieu of a security deposit is not a security deposit as defined in s. 83.43 (13). (7) A landlord has exclusive discretion as to whether to offer tenants the option to pay a fee in lieu of a security deposit and is not required to offer such fee option to tenants. However, if a landlord offers a tenant an option to pay a fee in lieu of a security deposit, the landlord may not use a prospective tenant’s choice to pay, or offer to pay, a fee in lieu of a security deposit as criteria in the determination to approve or deny an application for occupancy, and the landlord must also offer all new tenants renting a dwelling unit on the same premises the option to pay a fee in lieu of a security deposit, unless the landlord chooses to prospectively terminate the fee option for all new rental agreements. answer:
**Short answer:** you're entitled to the whole $1,050 unless the landlord sends a proper notice of a claim in time. Whether the landlord's time has already run out is not settled, and I can't lean either way.

**Your notice before leaving: met.** Because you left before the lease ended, 83.49(5) required at least "7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating," including an address where you can be reached. Your certified letter went out June 1 and the office signed for it June 3. The last day for notice was 2026-06-08, so you were in time. The letter gave your new address, and the lease (§7) allows certified mail to the office. The lease sets no different rule for leaving early. This means the landlord is not excused from the claim-notice requirement.

**No notice of a claim: met.** Under 83.49(3)(a), a landlord who wants to keep any of the deposit must send written notice of its claim and the reason for it, "by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address" or by e-mail under a signed addendum. Your lease (§8) says you did not agree to e-mail notices. You've received nothing by any means.

**The 30 days: not settled.** Section 83.49(3)(a) gives the landlord 30 days "after the termination of the rental agreement." Which date ends the rental agreement when you leave early is open.
- **Move-out date reading:** The disclosure in 83.49(2)(d) says the notice comes "within 30 days after you move out." Counting from your June 15 move-out, the 30 days ended 2026-07-15 and have passed. On this reading the landlord has forfeited any claim and must return the full deposit now.
- **Lease-end reading:** Section 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement," which treats vacating and termination as two separate things. Counting from the lease end on July 31, the 30 days run to 2026-08-30, which has not passed. On this reading the landlord can still send a timely claim notice until then.

**If the landlord misses the deadline:** under 83.49(3)(a), the landlord "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." So you would get all $1,050 back, but the landlord could still sue you for damages afterward. Early termination is the kind of thing a landlord might claim for.

**If a claim notice does arrive:**
- You would have 15 days after receiving it to object (83.49(3)(b)).
- If you don't object, the landlord may deduct the claim and must send you the balance within 30 days after the date of the notice.
- Missing the 15 days doesn't stop you from suing later for a refund.

**If anyone sues:** under 83.49(3)(c), the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney fee, and the court hears the case sooner.

Loaded deposit_not_returned. Its instructions:

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

answer:
**No, you can't ignore the e-mail. On the facts you've confirmed, it counts as the landlord's notice of its claim, and your deadline to object is close.**

**Why the e-mail counts**
- The statute allows a deposit-claim notice by certified mail or by e-mail. The e-mail route applies if the parties signed an addendum agreeing to electronic notices and each gave an e-mail address (83.49(3)(a); 83.505(1)).
- You and the landlord signed that addendum on July 10, 2025, and lease §8 lists an e-mail address for each of you. The landlord sent the notice to your listed address.
- Certified mail is not also required. The e-mail is an alternative to it.
- A notice sent by e-mail is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent" (83.505(4)).
- The notice was sent on August 20, which is inside the 30 days after your lease ended. That 30th day is August 30, and the e-mail came before it.
- The e-mail also states the amount ($400), the reason (carpet replacement), the 15-day deadline to object, and where to send the objection.
- So you can't claim the full deposit on the ground that the notice was defective. The landlord has not lost its claim on that ground.

**What happens next**
- **Your deadline to object:** You have 15 days after receiving the notice to object (83.49(3)(b)). You read it on August 20, so that counts to **September 4, 2026**. Today is September 2, so that date has not passed.
- **If you don't object:** The landlord may deduct the $400. It must send you the rest ($650) within 30 days of the notice date, which is **September 19, 2026** (83.49(3)(b)). Missing the deadline does not waive your right to sue later for a refund (83.49(3)(b)).
- **If you do object:** The statute gives no step after an objection except a court action. Whether the landlord can still deduct while you dispute it is not settled.
- **If someone sues:** The winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney's fee. The court also moves the case up on its calendar (83.49(3)(c)).

**Whether the carpet was your fault**
The statute doesn't decide that. It only sets the notice and objection procedure. Your objection is how you contest the claim and the amount, so object in writing.

**How to send it**
- The landlord's notice says to send the objection to the office address.
- Lease §7 says written notices to the landlord go "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or by certified mail to that address.
- With two days left, hand delivery is safest. Keep a copy and get a dated receipt or a witness.
- The addendum may also let you e-mail the objection to office@marshcreekpm.example.com. Send it that way too, if the addendum covers it.

**One gap**
I haven't seen the addendum's text. The statute requires it to say that e-mail notice is voluntary and can be revoked at any time (83.505(1)). If it doesn't, whether the e-mail counts as proper notice would be a different question. I'd still object by September 4 either way.

Does the addendum say anything about e-mail being voluntary or about revoking it?

Loaded deposit_not_returned. Its instructions:

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

answer:
**Probably yes, but one point is open.** If Florida's residential landlord-tenant law (ch. 83, part II) covers your housing, you get the whole $1,050 back. Your lease has an enrollment clause, and I need to settle whether it takes your housing outside that law.

**Why the whole deposit is owed if the law applies**
- **No notice of a claim.** To keep any of the deposit, the landlord had to send you written notice of its claim and the reason. It had to go by certified mail to your last known mailing address, or by e-mail if you had signed an e-mail addendum. It had to arrive "within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). You confirmed you got nothing, by any means.
- **The 30 days have run out.** Your lease ended July 31, 2026 (lease §3). The 30 days ended on 2026-08-30, which has passed. You moved out on the lease end date, so there is no question about which date starts the count.
- **You didn't have to give notice before leaving.** The 7-day notice rule in 83.49(5) applies only to tenants who leave before the lease term ends or who have a periodic tenancy. You stayed to the end of a fixed term.

The statute says that if the landlord misses the deadline, it "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant" (83.49(3)(a)). So the landlord owes you all of the deposit. It could still sue you for damages afterward, but it can't deduct them from your deposit.

If either of you goes to court over the deposit, "the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." The court is also required to "advance the cause on the calendar" (83.49(3)(c)). Only the winner gets costs and fees.

**The open point: the enrollment clause**
Part II does not apply to "residency or detention in a facility... when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services" (83.42(1)). Your landlord is a private management company, and the lease names no school as owner or manager. But lease §11 requires you to be enrolled at Alachua Valley College. It lets the landlord ask for proof of enrollment and end the lease if you aren't enrolled. That leaves enough doubt that I can't say the exclusion doesn't apply. If your housing is school housing, part II and its deposit rules would not apply, and I couldn't tell you the result under this statute. If it is an ordinary apartment with an enrollment condition, the answer above stands.

Is Lakeview Terrace run by or for Alachua Valley College, or could you live there only while you were enrolled there?

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).

**Yes, they had to send you the $650, and it's overdue. No, the $400 isn't gone for good, though you gave up the easy way to contest it.**

**The $650**
- The landlord's letter was sent by certified mail to the forwarding address you gave. It states the amount ($400), the reason (carpet replacement), the 15-day deadline to object, and where to send the objection. I see no defect in it. Under 83.49(3)(a), a landlord must send that notice within 30 days after the rental agreement ends. The 30 days ran through 2026-08-30, and the letter is dated 2026-08-20. So you can't claim the whole $1,050 on the ground that the notice came late or in the wrong form.
- Under 83.49(3)(b), if the tenant doesn't object, the landlord "may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages."
- Counting from the 2026-08-20 notice date, that 30-day deadline was 2026-09-19. It has passed, and you haven't been paid the balance.

**The $400**
- Your 15 days to object, counted from when you received the letter on 2026-08-24, ended 2026-09-08. Because you didn't object, the landlord was allowed to keep the $400.
- But 83.49(3)(b) also says: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." You can still sue to get the $400 back. Missing the deadline doesn't decide whether the carpet charge was fair. It only means the landlord could keep the money without a fight first.

**Going to court**

Loaded deposit_not_returned. Its instructions:

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

answer:
**No, not automatically.** The landlord has missed the deadlines, but in your situation that doesn't force it to return the whole deposit. You still keep your right to the deposit.

**Why the deadlines don't settle it for you**
- **The deadlines have passed.** The landlord had to return the deposit within 15 days after the rental ended if it wasn't claiming any of it (83.49(3)(a)). That date was 2026-09-15. If it meant to claim some of it, it had to send written notice within 30 days, and that date was 2026-09-30 (83.49(3)(a)). Your tenancy ended on the day you moved out, so the date is the same whichever way it is counted. You've had no notice of a claim. Normally that means the landlord "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit" (83.49(3)(a)).
- **Month-to-month tenants must give written notice before leaving.** A month-to-month tenant "must give at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating," and the notice must include an address where the tenant can be reached (83.49(5)). Your lease doesn't set a different rule for leaving. Clause 3 says only that the tenancy continues "until ended by Tenant or Landlord." Clause 7 says written notices go by hand to the office or by certified mail.
- **Your notice was oral.** Telling the manager in person on July 20 was not written notice. Handing in your forwarding address on August 31 was too late to count, because it came on the day you left.
- **The effect of missing that notice.** Missing the notice "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it" (83.49(5)). So the landlord's silence did not cost it a claim against the deposit. The statute also doesn't say you lose the deposit. You still have the right to it.

**What this means in practice**
- The landlord has not returned any of the $1,050 and has given no reason for keeping it. The statute doesn't say how much of it a landlord in this position may keep without sending notice. I can't tell you the whole $1,050 is owed, and I can't tell you the landlord may keep any of it.
- If either side sues over the deposit, "the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." The court is also required to "advance the cause on the calendar," which means it hears the case sooner (83.49(3)(c)).
